endorsements.quote: When selecting algorithms for reuse, investigators should pay close attention to the original development context and any filters applied to the source population.
Therefore, investigators should always be prepared to perform at least a minimal validation of the algorithm at their site to confirm it is fit for their purpose.
If the algorithm does not perform as expected then it should be modified and revalidated until it achieves the desired performance.

unlisted_practices: Investigators should review the specific population targeted and the validation definition used during initial development before selecting an existing phenotyping algorithm for reuse.
Investigators should identify which performance measures matter most for their application context before selecting a phenotyping algorithm.
Investigators should check for hidden influencers in algorithm design that cause a mismatch between the captured population and the stated target population.
Investigators should assess the availability and ambiguity of the source algorithm, and whether the data, technology and expertise needed to implement it exist at the reuse site.
Investigators should perform more robust validation studies for algorithms that have not been previously validated or have no reported performance characteristics.
Investigators should recognize possible phenotype misclassification and adapt usage accordingly when they cannot validate an algorithm locally.
Multi-site consortia should align on fitness-for-use goals (intended population and appropriate performance) before allowing site-specific customization of a shared algorithm.
Users of data-only phenotyping should report the uncertainty in algorithm accuracy and use sensitivity analyses to bound appropriate performance.
The field should develop reporting guidelines and metadata standards for phenotyping algorithms and phenotype libraries.

screen.reason: The paper introduces PhenoFit, a conceptual framework and guideline for evaluating whether computable phenotyping algorithms are fit for purpose and reuse across health systems.
